content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a fully-connected variant of MgNet for long-term time series forecasting. Their method delivers good performance compared to a set of baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts:
- The proposed method achieves reasonably strong performance when compared to a set of baselines.

Weaknesses:
- The paper is quite hard to follow. In particular, presenting a resonably complex architecture is simpler when a schematic is added to the paper. The motivations could also, in my opinion, be made clearer.
- The paper is quite derivative of MgNet. This is of course fully acknowledged in the submission, but this means that novelty is somewhat limited.
- A few missing baselines, most notably FreDO [1]. 
- A mention is made of using hierarchical features for time-series data in the submission. There are a set of papers that do that, the most recent being (if I am not mistaken) [2], but many examples exist in the past. They should be ideally mentioned and compared to.




References
[1] Frequency Domain-based Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
[2] Scaleformer: Iterative Multi-scale Refining Transformers for Time Series Forecasting

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes two approaches within the class of iterative methods constrained linear model methods for time-series forecasting. Specifically, the authors propose a fully connected version of the MgNet method used for vision tasks. Further, motivated by the V-cycle structure of multigrid methods the authors propose a V-cycle MgNet method called FV-MgNet. Experiments on six real-world datasets illustrate the promise of the approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

1. The lower memory requirements, faster inference speed, and prediction performance over long forecasting horizons are useful attributes of the method. 
2. The experiments are extensive and the ablation studies provide some insight into the contribution of the individual components. 

### Weaknesses

#### 1. Unsubstantiated Claims

The paper makes unsubstantiated claims in many places:

- At a concept level, this deals with interpretability. The paper does not explain or investigate empirically why their model is interpretable. Presumably, I'm guessing the linear nature of the model makes it interpretable. However, this is an arbitrary notion of interpretability and not even explained in the paper. See [R1] for a general discussion of the problem with arbitrary notions of interpretability and [R2] for a specific discussion on notions of interpretability applied to forecasting. 

[R1] The Mythos of Model Interpretability - Lipton

[R2] Why Did This Model Forecast This Future? Closed-Form Temporal Saliency Towards Causal Explanations of Probabilistic Forecasts - Raman et al. 

- "It is crucial to solving the linear equation 4 with a nonlinear constraint equation 5" Why?

- "For example, Figure 2 shows three typical examples in three different data sets, which can vary significantly in frequencies and amplitudes. Thus, convolution operators cannot process these different data sets uniformly." I don't see why the claim follows naturally from the statement about the complexity of the time series. Since the multi-level nature of the problem is important, as established and argued for in this paper, convolutional models that operate at multiple scales ought to be able to process data with the stated complexity. 

#### 2. Clarity and Motivation

As I specify in the next section, the clarity and writing of the paper can be improved. In many places the notations are not defined, and the modeling choices are insufficiently motivated, making them seem arbitrary, or based on unsubstantiated claims as stated above. Maybe these issues can be handled in writing, but prior to the rebuttal it is hard to evaluate this for me.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

The authors often introduce notation thay they don't explain. It is perhaps possible to guess what the notations mean, but this makes the paper less clear. E.g.
- In Eq. 6 $i$ probably denotes the iteration while $v$ denotes the total number of iterations, but this is not specified.
- In Eq. 5 the loop subscript is also $i$ but there it denotes a feature index.
- Likewise, in $R^I$ and $R^O$, $I$ and $O$ presumably refer to Input and Output dimensions, but I can imagine the lack of specification can be confusing for many.
- In Eq. 3 it also ought to specify that $\sigma(\cdot)$ refers to any activation function, not necessarily sigmoid.

Broadly, the motivations for the specific modeling choices need to be made stronger. Why is V-cycle a good idea? The authors only specify that they are inspired by the V-structure nature of Multigrid methods and that it is similar to a U-Net architecture. 

*But what part of the nature of the problem makes this a suitable idea?* For a paper that seeks to develop an interpretable method for forecsating can benefit from making this clear. 

### Quality

The experiments are extensive and the ablations support the argument of the paper. By addressing the unclear motivations and writing clarity the overall quality would be improved. 

### Novelty

The paper builds upon existing ideas applied to vision tasks. This is not necessarily a bad thing.  The paper says that it is the first time the MgNet type of method has been applied to the forecasting task, and I can't find any evidence to the contrary. 

### Reproducibility

I do not believe the code or trained models have been provided, so it is hard to reproduce results without implementing and training the method from scratch.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed methods produce promising results, the experiments are extensive, and the lower memory requirements and inference speed-up of the method are useful attributes. However, the unclear motivations and writing along with the lack of any supporting arguments for why the method is truly interpretable prevent me from recommending a higher score. Given the state of interpretable / explainable AI I believe making sound (and empirically-supported) claims about the interpretability of such methods is crucial.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work is about the problem of long-term time series forecasting. The authors propose a new class of fully connected V-cycle MgNet (which is a CNN model that was proposed for image classification based on the multigrain methods for solving discretized partial differential equations). They replace the convolutional operations with fully connected operations in the existing MgNet and apply them in forecasting problems. The also propose aV-cycle version of the fully connected MgNet to extract features hierarchically. More specifically, the authors propose to apply a constrained linear model for feature extraction. Then, they apply the fully connected operator as the underlying linear model, and finally, they introduce the multigrain structure to construct features in multi-resolution and reduce the computational complexity. The experimental setup included 5 comparison methods and 6 real-world datasets from various domains (electricity, economy, traffic, weather and disease). In most cases, the proposed model outperforms the rest of the models, using fewer parameters and with a faster inference speed. Results also improve as the length of the input sequence increases. Finally, an ablation study shows that the FV-MGNet structure is the best on among other variants.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper is about an interesting and difficult problem; long-term time-series forecasting.
- The authors have done a good job to cover the related works.
- The authors have done an extensive experimental analysis of the proposed model and other state of the art models in various datasets. They have included results to show the forecasting power of the models, the visualization of the forecasting output, the robustness experiment, an ablation study to investigate the structure of the model, and in the appendix they have included more analyses.

Weaknesses:
- The paper is hard to follow. For readers that are not familiar with the research area, it would be hard to understand the motivation, the challenges and the proposed methodology. This is not only because of the structure of the paper, but also because it is a hard topic that needs background knowledge of different areas. The authors can improve the writing by giving more motivation and challenges of the current state of the art models in the introduction and the related works section. The most important part to improve is the methodology section. A visualization of the overview of the proposed model will help the readers focus on one component for each sub-section. The authors can start by stating the general overview of the models and then focusing on why we need each step/component, what is the current methodology followed, how they change the current state of the art to serve better the needs of their application. Another easy edit that will improve the flow of the paper is to add the tables or figures in the pages that they are mentioned and not later in the text. For example, algorithm 1 is mentioned in page 3 and appears in page 6. Same “confusion” happens in the experiments section.
- The novelty of this work is incremental as it heavily relies on existing methodology from the related work.
- Are the results in Table 2 statistically significant? The differences in a few cases between the first and the second best model seem to be very close. It would be useful to add the significance scores and also move the table with the dataset statistics to the experimental setup of the main part of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There is space for improvement in the quality and the quality of this work, some suggestions can be found above in the weaknesses section. The novelty of the paper is incremental, however this is an interesting combination of known components that shows promising results. There is no mention regarding the reproducibility or making the code repository public upon acceptance. The authors do have implementation details in the paper and the appendix, but it would be hard to reproduce results without the authors’ code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper is about an interesting problem. The authors provide a promising direction for the long term time series forecasting problem. The paper is hard to read and improvements can be made. There are some questions about the results (please, check weaknesses), they do look promising though.
